title: GLAUCOMA CLINICAL MASTERY: FROM PATHOLOGY TO PERIOPERATIVE SURGERY
summary: An exhaustive clinical reference covering optic nerve anatomy, visual field analysis, medical therapeutics, and the management of high-stakes surgical complications. Designed for residents and fellows to master primary, secondary, and congenital glaucoma subtypes.

sections.title: Peripapillary Atrophy: Alpha vs. Beta Zones

branches: Alpha Zone (Outer): Irregular pigmentation and thinning of the Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE). Common and may be seen in normal eyes.
Beta Zone (Inner): Total atrophy of RPE and choriocapillaris. Visualization of large choroidal vessels and sclera. Highly associated with glaucomatous damage.
Clinical Significance: Beta zone presence and enlargement are strong predictors of glaucomatous progression and visual field loss.
Management: Monitor with objective longitudinal imaging (Stereoscopic photos or OCT) to detect RNFL changes and zone progression.
Differential Diagnosis: Myopic crescent (tilted disc) and historical chorioretinitis scars.

sections.title: Humphrey Visual Field (HVF) 24-2 & SITA FAST
content: Paracentral Scotomas: Localized field defects near fixation; typical signs of early glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
SITA FAST Algorithm: Swedish Interactive Threshold Algorithm designed for time-saving.
Rationale for SITA FAST: Reduces test time significantly by relying on probability estimation. Stops when sufficient data points are acquired.
Clinical Benefit: Mitigates patient fatigue and improves reliability for detecting subtle defects compared to older full-threshold techniques.
Functional-Structural Correlation: VF defects (function) must correlate with optic nerve changes (structure, e.g., OCT thinning).

sections.title: POAG Diagnostic Pearls
sections.content: Between 30% and 50% of individuals with glaucomatous optic neuropathy and/or visual field loss present with an initial IOP measurement below 22 mm Hg. This reflects that IOP can vary significantly over a 24-hour period. Differentiating Glaucoma from other neuropathies on MRI: Post-contrast enhancement of the optic nerve is NOT consistent with glaucoma and suggests inflammatory, infectious, or compressive etiologies.

sections.title: Medical Management: Prostaglandin Analogues (PGAs)
content: Step 1: Primary Pathway - PGAs lower IOP primarily by increasing uveoscleral outflow (pressure-insensitive).
Step 2: Mechanism - Binding to receptors triggers a cascade leading to remodeling of the ciliary body and uveoscleral tissues.
Step 3: Drug Selection - First-line therapy due to high efficacy and once-daily dosing.
Step 4: Intolerance Management - Switch to preservative-free agents or change drug classes (e.g., fixed combination Beta-blocker/CAI).
Step 5: Alternative - Offer Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT) as non-invasive control.

sections.title: NVG Clinical Protocol
content: Presentation: Rubeosis Iridis (NVI) and secondary angle closure.
Underlying Cause: Retinal ischemia triggers VEGF release.
Treatment (Disease): Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) and Intravitreal Anti-VEGF.
Treatment (IOP): Aqueous suppressants (Acetazolamide, Alpha agonists).
Surgery: Glaucoma Drainage Devices (GDD/Valves) if visual potential exists.
Blind Painful Eye: Cyclodestructive procedures (CPC/Cryo).

branches: Pseudoexfoliation (PXF): Deposition of dandruff-like material; most common cause of secondary OAG. Risk of zonular weakness and poor dilation in surgery.
Uveitis-Glaucoma-Hyphema (UGH) Syndrome: Caused by IOL dislocation or iris chafe. Manage with IOL repositioning or exchange.
Posner-Schlossman (Glaucomatocyclitic Crisis): Young male, pain, IOP 40s, mild uveitis, open angle. Associated with CMV/HSV. Treat with steroids + suppressants.
Silicone Oil Glaucoma: Migration of emulsified oil into AC or blocking meshwork. Requires oil removal or aqueous suppressants.
Steroid-Induced: Due to glycosaminoglycan deposition in trabecular meshwork; common in RA patients on long-term treatment.

sections.title: Primary Congenital Glaucoma (PCG)
content: Inheritance: Autosomal recessive in ~90% of cases.
Recurrence Risk: 1%–5% for siblings of affected child (or 0%–25% in clinical scenarios).
Triad: Epiphora, Photophobia, Blepharospasm.
Signs: Buphthalmos (enlarged globe), Corneal edema, Haab's striae (Descemet's breaks).
Examination: EUA (Exam Under Anesthesia) for IOP, corneal diameter, and pachymetry.
Surgery: Goniotomy or Trabeculotomy are preferred initial angle surgeries.

rows: Better safety profile; easier maintenance than trabeculectomy.

sections.title: Glaucoma Emergencies Checklist
content: Acute Secondary Glaucoma (IOP 40+) in soccer players (Traumatic Hyphema/Angle Recession).
Gas-induced Pupillary Block after Full-Thickness Macular Hole surgery.
Expulsive Choroidal Hemorrhage during cataract surgery (Acute shallow AC, high IOP).
Iris Bombe & Seclusio Pupillae in JRA Uveitis - requires urgent Peripheral Iridotomy (PI).
NPGS Contraindications: Neovascular, narrow angle, and congenital glaucoma.

sections.title: Advanced Glaucoma Presentation
sections.content: End-stage glaucoma is characterized by extensive peripheral vision loss, resulting in only a small central and temporal island remaining (Tunnel Vision). Examination often reveals a RAPD (Grade 1), signifying severe unilateral optic nerve damage. Optic atrophy types: Primary (follows retrobulbar lesion), Secondary (follows disc edema), Consecutive (follows chronic retinal disease), and Glaucomatous (rim loss and deep cupping).
